strengths: The paper identifies a real and under-discussed practical issue for learned lossless compression: encoder and decoder probability mismatch caused by nondeterministic neural inference can make arithmetic coding fail catastrophically.

The proposed PMATIC construction is simple, model-agnostic, and plausibly useful: quantizing conditional bit probabilities with helper bits gives an intuitive way for encoder and decoder to agree under a bounded mismatch model.
The formal setup is mostly clear, and the main correctness argument under a hard conditional-TV mismatch bound is easy to follow.

The experiments provide a proof of concept showing that the method can decode successfully under synthetic bounded logit perturbations and can retain much of the compression gain of an LLM-based compressor in that controlled setting.
weaknesses: The evaluation is far too limited for a top-tier acceptance. The central motivation is real LLM nondeterminism across hardware/software settings, but the experiments use only synthetic IID logit noise rather than measured real-world prediction mismatch. There is no evidence that the assumed hard global logit bound holds in practice.

The compression baselines are weak. Comparing only to gzip and a no-mismatch LLM compressor is insufficient; strong text compression baselines such as zstd, brotli, xz, cmix/nncp, and recent LLMZip/FineZip-style systems are needed. The claim of outperforming modern compression tools is therefore not adequately supported.

The reported compression ratios exclude the cost of the LLM, tokenizer, bitstring dictionary, runtime, and deployment assumptions. This is common in model-based compression studies, but the paper makes practical claims without quantifying model-size amortization, compute cost, memory, or speed.

The theoretical compression-loss analysis relies on strong simplifying assumptions, especially that next-bit probabilities are roughly uniformly distributed within bins. Without this, helper-bit overhead can be much larger than the stated estimate. The analysis is therefore not a robust bound on actual performance.

The novelty is somewhat incremental from an information-coding perspective: probability quantization plus side information is a natural robust-coding construction. The paper does not sufficiently position PMATIC against prior work on robust arithmetic coding, finite-precision arithmetic coding, synchronized coding, or quantized probability models.

The experiments are narrow: two text datasets, one quantized Llama model, two parameter settings, no ablations over r and delta, no measured failure rates for ordinary arithmetic coding under real mismatch, and no sensitivity analysis for mismatch magnitude or distribution.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper does not appear to release code, seeds, exact model variant/quantization details, random token-code dictionary construction, arithmetic-coding precision details, or enough implementation information to replicate the numbers reliably.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, especially that PMATIC is a practical drop-in replacement and that it addresses LLM nondeterminism as encountered in real systems. The paper currently supports a controlled proof of concept, not a demonstrated practical solution.

strengths: The paper identifies a real practical issue for neural model-driven lossless compression: arithmetic coding requires encoder and decoder probabilities to match exactly, while modern neural inference can be non-deterministic across hardware/software settings.

The proposed PMATIC mechanism is simple and model-agnostic: it quantizes conditional bit probabilities and uses helper bits so encoder and decoder can agree on a shared probability under a bounded mismatch assumption.
The paper gives a reasonably clear formalization of bounded prediction mismatch, including a correctness argument under conditional TV distance and a basic compression-loss analysis.

The experimental table shows that the implementation can decode successfully under the authors' synthetic bounded-noise setting and that the overhead decreases when the assumed mismatch bound is smaller.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is far too limited for a top-tier AI conference. The main result is a single table on two text datasets with only two mismatch settings, synthetic iid logit noise, and no real cross-hardware or cross-software nondeterminism experiment, despite real nondeterminism being the paper's central motivation.

The baseline comparison is weak and potentially misleading. The paper compares mainly to gzip and a no-mismatch Llama compressor, but omits strong compression baselines such as xz, zstd, brotli, cmix/NNCP, FineZip, LLMZip-style systems, and other neural compressors. Claiming superiority over modern compression tools from a gzip-only comparison is not supported.

The method's practical significance is unclear. The experiments use Llama 3.1 8B token probabilities but do not report runtime, memory, GPU cost, model-size assumptions, throughput, or end-to-end deployability. A compressor requiring repeated LLM inference may be impractical even if the nominal compressed bitstream is short.

The mismatch model is a strong hard bound on every logit at every context, and the paper does not show that real LLM nondeterminism satisfies this assumption or quantify realistic epsilon values. The future-work section explicitly acknowledges that validation on real-world mismatch is missing, which undercuts the central claim.

Several evaluation accounting details are underspecified or questionable: whether file lengths, token-bit dictionaries, metadata, chunk boundaries, arithmetic-coder finalization overhead, and model/tokenizer assumptions are counted; how random token-bit assignments affect results; and whether results are averaged over seeds.

The theoretical contribution is modest. Quantizing probabilities with side information to make arithmetic coding robust is intuitive, and the analysis relies on simplifying assumptions such as uniform placement within bins and true encoder probabilities. The paper does not establish optimality or compare to alternative robust coding schemes.

There are clarity and polish issues, including a likely typo in the helper-bit definition where the bit value is tested for membership in probability intervals, overstrong language about validation and modern tool superiority, and relatively shallow discussion of failure cases.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper does not appear to release code, gives sparse implementation detail for the Llama setup and arithmetic coding integration, and the appendix states substantial LLM assistance in writing and code development without enough accompanying artifacts to independently verify the implementation.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and under-discussed obstacle for model-driven lossless compression: encoder/decoder prediction mismatch caused by numerical non-determinism. This is a timely problem as neural and LLM-based compressors become more plausible.

PMATIC is conceptually simple, model-agnostic, and plausibly useful as a drop-in replacement for arithmetic coding when the prediction mismatch is bounded. The probability-matching formulation is clear and gives the paper a focused technical contribution.

The correctness argument is clean: the conditional-TV formulation naturally supports sequential bit conditioning, and the bin-center/boundary helper-bit mechanism gives an intuitive route to exact agreement between encoder and decoder.

The empirical results are encouraging as a proof of concept: under synthetic bounded logit perturbations, decoding succeeds and compression remains substantially better than gzip, with a sensible degradation as robustness increases.
The manuscript is generally readable and well-positioned with respect to neural compression and reproducibility/non-determinism concerns.
weaknesses: The experimental validation is too limited for a top-tier acceptance. The central motivation is real-world LLM non-determinism, but the experiments use only synthetic IID uniform logit noise; there is no measurement of actual cross-hardware, cross-library, mixed-precision, or nondeterministic inference mismatch.

The baselines are weak. Comparing mainly to gzip and a no-mismatch version of the same LLM compressor does not establish competitiveness against strong compressors such as zstd/xz/brotli, neural compressors, cmix/NNCP-style systems, LLMZip/FineZip/llama-zip variants, or robust alternatives such as deterministic inference/quantization/checkpointing strategies.

The practical story is incomplete. There is little discussion or measurement of runtime, memory, model storage assumptions, implementation complexity, or end-to-end throughput, which are crucial for LLM-driven compression and are explicitly mentioned as barriers in the introduction.

The theoretical compression-loss analysis relies on simplifying assumptions that are not fully validated, especially the approximate uniformity of next-bit probabilities within bins and the helper-bit entropy model. The paper should empirically test these assumptions and provide ablations over r and delta.

The robustness guarantee depends on a hard uniform mismatch bound over logits/conditional distributions, but real numerical variation may be stochastic, context-dependent, token-dependent, and occasionally large. The paper acknowledges this as future work, but it is central enough to weaken the main claim.

Some presentation and technical details need tightening. For example, the text appears to conflate the probability of being in a bin interior with the probability of being near a boundary when discussing helper bits, and the exact arithmetic-coding convention for helper-bit probabilities should be stated more carefully.

Reproducibility is not sufficiently established: the paper does not appear to provide code, detailed implementation choices, random seeds, hardware/software configurations, or enough information to reproduce the Llama-based compression pipeline precisely.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and under-discussed failure mode for model-driven lossless compression: tiny encoder/decoder prediction mismatches can catastrophically break arithmetic decoding.
PMATIC is conceptually simple, model-agnostic, and plausibly useful as a drop-in robust replacement for arithmetic coding in learned compression systems.
The theoretical framing is clear: the bounded logit mismatch to conditional TV argument, the correctness guarantee, and the compression-overhead tradeoff give a coherent foundation for the method.

Experiments cover several LLMs, datasets, and robustness settings, and they show the expected robustness/compression tradeoff as well as compelling qualitative failures of standard arithmetic coding under mismatch.
weaknesses: The evaluation of real nondeterminism is quite limited: only two Apple laptop configurations, one model, and a small subset of files. This is not enough to substantiate broad claims about robustness to practical LLM nondeterminism across hardware/software stacks.

The paper compares compressed file sizes against gzip/brotli/cmix etc. but does not account for the very large model storage, inference cost, latency, or deployment assumptions. Claims that PMATIC/LLM compression outperforms standard tools are therefore overstated for many practical settings.

There is no comparison to the closely related concurrent mismatch-tolerant coding approach beyond citation, and no strong baseline for robust coding besides standard arithmetic coding, which is expected to fail.

The compression-loss analysis relies on strong simplifying assumptions, especially the uniformity/helper-bit model, and the theoretical bound is relatively loose; the paper itself shows the assumption is inaccurate in practice.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: code availability, exact preprocessing, random longform dictionaries, quantization setup, model inference settings, and deterministic/non-deterministic backend details are not fully specified.

Several presentation and consistency issues reduce confidence, e.g. the text states a PMATIC setting of delta=0.1 with r=0.125 even though the table uses delta=1e-2 and the stated requirement r > 2 delta would be violated for delta=0.1; Eq. 13 also appears to define the helper bit using the token bit rather than the predicted probability.
The scope is narrow: the method is evaluated only on text compression, while many motivating claims refer broadly to model-driven compression and other domains.

strengths: The paper identifies a real practical issue for model-driven lossless compression: encoder/decoder probability mismatch from nondeterministic neural inference can catastrophically break arithmetic decoding.

The proposed PMATIC idea is simple and model-agnostic: quantize conditional bit probabilities and transmit helper bits so encoder and decoder agree on a shared coding distribution under bounded mismatch.

The paper includes a formal problem setup, a correctness theorem under conditional-TV/logit mismatch assumptions, and experiments covering several LLMs, datasets, robustness settings, and both synthetic and limited real hardware mismatch.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not convincing for a top-tier AI venue. The real nondeterminism experiment is very small, uses only two Apple laptop configurations and a limited set of files, and does not rigorously characterize mismatch distributions, failure probabilities, or robustness margins.

The synthetic mismatch experiment is largely tautological: noise is chosen to satisfy the theorem’s assumptions, so successful decoding mainly verifies the implementation rather than demonstrating robustness in realistic or adversarial settings.

The compression comparisons are potentially misleading. Reported ratios exclude model storage, inference cost, latency, and deployment constraints, even though these dominate practical LLM-based compression. Claims of outperforming standard compressors are therefore overstated.

Reproducibility is weak: datasets are partly described as randomly selected Wikipedia articles from a particular date, implementation details are incomplete, code availability is not stated, random token-longform assignments are used, and model quantization/configuration details are underspecified.

Theoretical analysis relies on strong assumptions that are not validated in practice, especially bounded conditional TV distance for every context and token. The real mismatch setting appears stochastic and occasionally outside the bound, which the method does not theoretically handle.

The compression-loss analysis is approximate and rests on a questionable uniformity assumption over bin locations; the paper’s own Table 2 shows the assumption is inaccurate, yet the method still uses it for helper-bit coding.

The algorithm introduces arbitrary fixed-length random bit representations for tokens, but the effect of this choice on compression efficiency, variance, unused codewords, and reproducibility is not adequately analyzed.

Several presentation and technical details are sloppy, including notation errors such as defining the helper bit using the token bit rather than the predicted probability, inconsistent parameter text, and occasional overclaims about being a drop-in arithmetic-coding replacement.

The work is positioned as addressing LLM nondeterminism, but it does not compare against direct deterministic inference backends, fixed CPU inference, probability rounding/serialization, checksum/resynchronization schemes, or other simpler engineering baselines.
Overall, while the core idea is plausible, the paper does not provide enough evidence, rigor, or practical analysis to support its strong claims or justify acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and practically relevant failure mode for neural/model-driven lossless compression: tiny encoder-decoder probability mismatches can catastrophically break arithmetic decoding. The framing is timely given increasing use of LLMs as predictive compressors.
PMATIC is conceptually simple, model-agnostic, and well explained. The bin/interior/helper-bit construction gives a clear mechanism for forcing agreement between encoder and decoder probabilities.

The theoretical part is a real contribution: the paper formalizes bounded mismatch via conditional TV distance, relates logit perturbations to this notion, proves correctness under the bound, and gives an interpretable compression-overhead analysis.

The empirical results support the main qualitative claim: PMATIC preserves decoding under synthetic bounded perturbations and succeeds on a small real cross-device nondeterminism experiment where standard arithmetic coding fails.

The compression results suggest that the robustness overhead is moderate for small mismatch levels, and the helper-bit analysis is useful because it points to a concrete route for improving efficiency.
weaknesses: The real nondeterminism evaluation is too small for the strength of the claims: it uses one model family, two Apple laptops, short files, and limited datasets. A top-tier paper should test more hardware/software pairs, model sizes, precisions, decoding backends, and longer files where rare mismatch violations are more likely.

The bounded worst-case mismatch assumption is clean but may not match real neural inference, where occasional outlier logit differences can occur. The paper acknowledges this, but the practical guarantee depends critically on choosing δ, and there is no systematic method for estimating or certifying δ in deployment.

The comparison to traditional compressors is not fully satisfying. The paper does not include model size, shared tokenizer/dictionary costs, runtime/latency, or energy, and the reported baselines for tools such as cmix/xz appear weaker than expected for standard text-compression benchmarks. This weakens the claim of outperforming modern compression tools.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the paper does not clearly state code/data release status, exact compressor commands, random seeds/longform dictionaries, tokenizer handling, or whether all preprocessing is identical across baselines.

The overhead analysis relies on simplifying assumptions, especially the within-bin uniformity/helper-bit model. The empirical helper-bit results show the assumption is inaccurate, which is useful but also means the theoretical rate prediction is only loosely validated.
The paper is positioned against concurrent Hu & Tang work but gives little technical comparison. It is hard to judge the novelty and tradeoffs of PMATIC relative to that closest related approach.

Some presentation issues remain, including a few typos/inconsistencies such as the helper-bit definition appearing to condition on the token bit rather than the predicted probability, and duplicated/mislabeled dataset enumeration. These are minor but should be cleaned up.
